inline.s: My mother was the youngest daughter of Lord Zeng Wenzheng (Zeng Guofan). The family rule of Lord Wenzheng stipulated that the expense for marrying off a daughter or taking in a bride must be limited to within two hundred taels. When my mother married, several years had already passed since the passing of Lord Wenzheng and his wife; the three thousand taels of her dowry was also transferred aside and used for household expenses and for making good the money that a certain money house had cheated from my grandmother, until my mother's own savings were entirely exhausted. When she left her home in Hunan and headed east, my grandmother could furnish only six hundred taels of silver for travel expenses, and beyond that there was nothing at all. In her middle years, whenever my mother spoke of those hard times, tears would fall with her words; that she, a daughter of noble and ministerial rank, married into a great household of officials spanning many generations, and yet lived in such straitened circumstances — had it not been personally experienced, it would truly be hard to believe!

The reason I take such pains to recount these trivial, wordy details is to prove the profound truth of the saying that the benevolent use wealth to establish themselves, rather than using themselves to amass wealth — it truly carries deep and far-reaching meaning! What we should note here is this: though this was poverty for several generations, yet it was exchanged for the prosperity of later descendants! Compared with those who leave behind much property to harm their descendants, feeding their arrogance, extravagance, and idleness until their children sink into ruin, the difference between the two is truly as wide as heaven and earth! Lord Zeng Wenzheng gave the house where he lived the name of the Study of Seeking Imperfection (Qiuque Zhai) and even wrote an essay to record it. His intent was to hold fast to fullness and guard against overflow, to remain vigilant even in times of peace! For in this world there is no such thing as perfect completeness; those who are rich in one thing are certain to be lacking in another. Therefore, if one wishes to attain spiritual completeness, it is best to have constant small lack in material things.

By spiritual completeness, I mean that both parents are still living, the family is harmonious, and the descendants are worthy, wise, and intelligent, enjoying the happiness of family love and the joy of righteousness. By material things, I mean clothing and food, carriages and horses, palaces and dwellings, and even official rank and wealth — all manner of enjoyments. Lord Zeng Wenzheng often used this principle to teach his family, saying that family finances should not be too ample — this is exactly opposite to the common view. Lord Wenzheng often said further: the ancients had the saying that the blossom is not yet fully open and the moon not yet full — this is the state of the wise; for once the blossom is fully open, it means it will soon wither; and once the moon is full, in an instant it is about to wane! So-called prosperity at its peak must decline, and joy at its limit breeds sorrow. Could it be that the ancients delighted in speaking these words that sound so unpleasant and unpleasing in the ears of their hearers? No — these words are all truth! And from ancient times to the present, observing the phenomena of society, these words have not been wrong! And they hold without a single exception!

A proverb also says: “no family stays rich for three generations,” and again: “there is no feast under heaven that does not break up.” The wise realize this truth deeply, so when they handle affairs, they first consider: do not seek excessive completeness in anything, and do not let things become too flourishing and go over the top. For the gathering and scattering of wealth they make sound and complete plans; and for their own lives they follow the causal law of maintaining fullness and preserving prosperity; personal enjoyments should not be lavish; and they always bear in mind the poor who are homeless in the streets and without food for three meals a day! Always think of the charitable halls in various places, of the corpses left to lie in the open, of how exceedingly numerous are the suffering people! I should economize my own enjoyments to save the dying and console the orphaned. For a single thought of compassion can give rise to a spirit of harmony and peace between heaven and earth; and as it is put into action, this spirit of peace will often gather around me, and can bring benediction upon my family and descendants. As for these truths, only by carefully studying the facts both ancient and modern can one understand that these words are true and not false!

Conversely, if one knows only to indulge in one's own pleasures, heedless of the lives, deaths, suffering, and pain of others; using deceit and scheming to seize by craft and to plunder by force, and angling by every device — such a person may amass a great deal of money and may hold great power; those who flatter and praise him may be beyond counting; for a time he seems exceedingly lofty and distinguished. Yet the waxing and waning, the fullness and emptiness, of Heaven's Way has its own unchanging principle!

Thirty or fifty years pass in the blink of an eye; time constantly presses forward, and scenes constantly shift and change! What was once a humble lane in cold obscurity suddenly rises to become a parvenu; yet prosperity does not last, and the splendid household declines and fades in a single fleeting instant! For in this world there is nothing firm and imperishable, and no enterprise that can be forever dependable; all wealth and status gained by craft and plunder will surely be squandered and lost all the more swiftly! Only families of filial piety, brotherly love, sincerity, and generosity, and descendants who cultivate virtue and accumulate goodness, can truly preserve their estate and make it great and long-lasting! The records of such events in the annals of history are many, and looking around at the affairs happening about us, they are everywhere! So those with a cool head and wisdom will naturally see it.

blocks.text: Appendix 2: The Guiding Influence of Official Conduct Must Be Valued

inline.s: In recent times the extravagant customs of society have grown very strong, and this dissipating trend can exert an extremely harmful influence upon politics. As to this principle, Master Gu Tinglin, the great scholar of the Ming dynasty, perceived it long ago and once wrote a special essay citing many historical facts. I now respectfully copy these facts below for the reference of those who study government.

If the customs of the nation and the society grow extravagant, those who govern should shift the prevailing trend by honoring frugality and simplicity. The Book of Rites says: “the conduct of the gentleman is the standard by which the prime minister spreads good governance.” This means that the actions of each of us can also influence the politics of the nation. Master Gu Tinglin pointed out even more plainly: “for the safety or peril of the empire, even the humblest common man shares the responsibility.” This is the same meaning.

In the Eastern Han dynasty, Xu Shao of Runan commandery held office there as a local official; and Yuan Shao, of the same commandery, had an extremely large retinue of horses and attendants. But whenever Yuan Shao reached the border of the commandery, he would dismiss his accompanying horsemen and drive home alone in a single carriage, saying: “how could I let Master Xu Shao see my retinue of carriages and attendants!”

Cai Chong of the Jin dynasty was fond of study and well known for it. At that time, Liu Zheng of Gaoping was exceedingly extravagant and splendid in his carriages and clothing; but Liu Zheng once said to others: “although I have the bad habit of liking to wear splendid clothing, yet whenever I meet Cai Chong and sit with him, that day my heart cannot help feeling uneasy all day long, and I feel that I am truly vulgar and unrefined!”

Li Delin of the Northern Qi, when his father passed away, walked on foot carrying his father's coffin back to his home in Boling for burial, and the funeral was very simple. His friend Cui Chen went to offer condolences, with a retinue of several dozen men on horseback. To honor Li Delin's spirit of frugality, Cui Chen steadily reduced the number of his attendants along the way. By the time he reached the gate of the Li family, only five attendants remained, and he said: “I must not let my friend, Brother Li, mistake me for a man of arrogant and overbearing ways.”

Li Sengjia lived in seclusion in the mountains; at that time the court issued an edict summoning him to take office, but Li Sengjia declined and was unwilling to assume the post. The Minister Yuan Shude went to visit Li Sengjia, and likewise reduced his accompanying servants along the way, saying: “to visit a worthy of such lofty wisdom and detachment as Master Li would make me ashamed before my own splendid carriages and official robes!” Thus, the noble conduct of a gentleman — if he holds office in a locality, he can guide and transform one region; if he holds office at court, he can civilize the whole empire.

In the Dali era of the Tang dynasty, the emperor issued a decree appointing Yang Wan as prime minister. Yang Wan, in office, had always been incorruptible, upright, and clean in conduct, and he lived a very frugal life. At the time, the Censor-in-Chief Cui Kuan was exceedingly wealthy with many possessions; the pavilions, towers, terraces, and bowers in his household garden were not only numerous but beautiful, and at the time were called the finest under heaven. But when he heard the news that Yang Wan had become prime minister, that very day he silently tore down the pavilions and towers in his garden. And when Guo Ziyi heard that Yang Wan had taken office as prime minister, he also cut his household musicians by four-fifths. You should know that Guo Ziyi's military merits were great — he had rendered a mighty service by recovering the two imperial capitals and was ennobled by the emperor as the Prince of Fenyang; his prestige and power might be said to have startled the age. Yet he stood in such awe of a prime minister who honored integrity and simplicity! What a pity that today we can no longer see officials such as Yang Wan, nor figures such as Cui Kuan and Guo Ziyi.

Li Shigu relied upon his armed forces and behaved quite tyrannically, often defying the court's commands; yet he stood in fear of the prime minister Huang Shang. Li Shigu once ordered a capable confidant of his, bearing several thousand taels of gold, to go to the Huang household bearing gifts in the hope of forming a connection. The confidant, arriving at the gate of the Huang home, happened to meet a sedan chair coming out of the prime minister's residence; beside it there were only two maidservants walking on foot, and their clothing was very humble indeed, and they said the person seated within was the prime minister's wife. The confidant, being exceedingly alert, understood at once the clean, frugal ways of the prime minister and dared not rashly enter the residence with the gifts, so he brought the gold back and hurried home, reporting in detail all that he had seen and heard to Li Shigu. Because of this, Li Shigu stood in even greater awe of Huang Shang, and changed his former intention to rebel; to the end of his days he submitted to the court's commands and never again dared to disobey.

From the above examples, one can see that when persons of both moral excellence and learning serve as local officials, the locality obtains blessing; and when the officials at the center are incorruptible and upright, the whole nation gains its benefit. So the mutual influence between honoring integrity and frugality and government is truly very close! The ancients said: “only frugality can nurture integrity.” And its opposite — extravagance — cannot but give rise to corruption, and the result of corruption will certainly throw society and the empire into great disorder. The Great Learning also says: “in the production of wealth there is a great Way: those who produce it are many, those who consume it are few; those who make it are diligent, those who use it are unhurried — then wealth will always be sufficient.” This is a law of economics, like a formula in mathematics, that cannot be changed! Today the customs of society are rotten, with everyone competing to worship the West and aping the bad habits of Europe and America; in clothing, footwear, food and drink, and all enjoyments there is nothing but the utmost extravagance and luxury, with a thousand taels spent at the drop of a hat. When the prevailing trend exerts such an influence, how can politics not fall into disorder?

For my own part, I believe that our nation has always been one that honors frugality and simplicity, and those good old customs urgently ought to be preserved; toward European and American civilization, we should choose and discriminate, and not accept everything wholesale. Some may say that I am driving in reverse, but when one meets a road that cannot be traveled, to advance is dangerous; at such a time the only course is to back up quickly in order to save one's life and to seek a better path by other means — what is wrong with that? I hope the worthy and distinguished of the present age will not be sparing of their instruction.
Nie Yuntai, November 1947

blocks.text: Appendix 3: Benefiting Others and Aiding the World Is the Root of Preserving Blessings

inline.s: Excerpted from Layman Yuntai's Nighttime Jottings While Confined to Bed with Illness

Wealth comes, and we do not sense it coming; wealth departs, and we do not sense it leaving. Though one exhausts all scheming, it is truly wasted effort! This principle, and the karma within it, is quite complex and not easy to understand. If anyone can thoroughly comprehend it, he must surely be a person of great wisdom.

For all good deeds, the crucial point lies in the aspiration; the amount of money is of secondary importance. If the aspiration is genuine but one's strength is insufficient, then though the money be little, the merit is exceedingly great; and if one lacks a true mind of compassion, though the money be much, the merit is very small. As for whether children are wise or foolish, worthy or unworthy, the influence of education is truly limited! As for the strength or weakness of a child's physique and the length or shortness of its life, even medicine and hygiene are not the decisive factors! One must instead cultivate a heart of compassion within oneself and always take benefiting others and aiding the world as the goal of one's conduct. If one does so, then descendants may enjoy happiness and attain complete fulfillment. I hope the reader can understand and accept this principle and idea, and cultivate blessings for one's children!

A descendant's learning and career are entirely influenced by the virtue and blessings accumulated by his ancestors and parents; if the forebears built the family upon meanness and cruelty, then even if a descendant's studies succeed by good luck, in the end he will never prosper for long. Everyone shares the wish that his own descendants will flourish, yet the result is for the most part the exact opposite. Why? Because none of them understand the principle that “the family that accumulates goodness will surely have surplus joy; the family that accumulates evil will surely have surplus calamity”!

If one wishes to know the method of cultivating a compassionate heart, one must first understand the principle of karmic retribution; and these two books, The Ancient Mirror of Moral Education and The Four Teachings of Liaofan, must be kept constantly upon one's desk and read often, so that a good heart may be preserved and not fade from forgetfulness.

In recent years, criminologists of various countries, from the crime statistics of those countries, have discovered that the Netherlands has the fewest criminal offenders. The report says: that nation's sole distinguishing feature lies in its emphasis upon propriety and teaching, and the separation between men and women is very strict. For example, in the Jewel City near The Hague, there is a regulation that in public places men and women are not permitted to sit together within six feet; and the prison of that city stands empty the year round, without a single prisoner. The criminologists say: all crime arises from the weakness of the criminal's willpower, that is, an unsound mind. The facts of the Netherlands prove that the restraint of sexual desire can keep the people's minds clearer and more healthy, so that they do not commit crime. Thus our nation's propriety and teaching, which makes the separation of men and women especially strict — the so-called that men and women have their separate spheres — truly has its scientific basis.

In the past thirty years the number of crimes in America has surged, and ten years ago it leapt to first place in the world. The licentiousness between men and women in America is truly the most conspicuous of all, and dancing is the most common of all. In recent years American newspapers have repeatedly reported that in some American university, upon physical examination, it was found that more than half of the female students were no longer virgins. According to American crime reports, in the single year of 1939 the number of those who committed morals offenses suddenly rose by seven percent. Over the past six years, rape cases have sharply increased by fifty percent. J. Edgar Hoover, director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, once declared: “young people's moral decline and the increase of crime are truly the result brought about by the saturation of pornographic publications.” Mr. Lorous, a prison officer, said: “the many cases I have handled have all been influenced by pornographic publications.” Mr. Bates, director of the United States Federal Bureau of Prisons, declared: “the sharp increase in criminal cases is entirely due to newspapers printing very many morals cases, and to the influence of films and pornographic publications.” Director Hoover also said: “America is now working hard to eradicate these obscene publications.” It is a pity he still does not know that the harm of dancing is even greater than that of pornographic publications!

Taking a comprehensive view of the above, the spread of pornographic publications and dancing has actually brought society down to such a state of decline. Because sexual desire is a common instinct of animals, which have a natural period of restraint, while humans have thought. Yet since humans, through the contact of the eyes and ears, are stirred by their emotions, only by strictly defining ritual law and avoiding the opportunities of contact can one reduce the stirrings of human desire. Laozi said: “not seeing what is desirable keeps the heart from disorder.” In other words, seeing what is desirable makes the heart easily disturbed. Europeans and Americans advocate the liberation of men and women, open social intercourse, coeducation of the sexes, and revealing dress; no greater desire of the human heart is there than this. Therefore our New Culture advocates, who argue for accepting Western culture wholesale, instead bitterly denounce our nation's inherent fine traditions as the old cannibalistic propriety, and wish to overthrow them all. The main purpose of this liberation of sexual desire is to make women easy for men to toy with and trample upon, to gratify their wills and satisfy their desires. This causes many women to be lured and entrapped by men, and once fallen, they hastily and reluctantly marry. Hence divorce cases are surging throughout the whole world, and they are most numerous of all in America. In 1925, American divorces numbered two hundred thousand. More than a decade ago I once wrote an article discussing this matter. Observing the degeneration of the American female students described above, one knows that the many divorces are because the original marriages were formed by the impulse of physical-emotional passion — a choice without reason! From the standpoint of eugenics, these parents who are united purely by sexual desire, without any deep foundation of affection, will surely give birth to children who lack sound willpower, and even more lack deep reason and mind. In a nation, if there be many such parents, there will likewise be many people of weak will and deficient reason. That America has so much crime, and the Netherlands so little — this is the proof of the facts.

As for morals offenses, most of them arise from the enticement of pornographic publications and the emotional impulses occasioned by dancing. These are due to the offender's temporary loss of the power of will and choice, and not entirely to some innate deficiency in the offender. As for ordinary criminal offenses — such as fraud, fighting, robbery, armed robbery, and murder — these are caused by the offender's innate weakness of willpower and lack of reason and intelligence. For example, the Netherlands is very strict in separating men and women, and all criminal offenses there are extremely few; while the Jewel City, strictest of all in ritual defense, has its prison empty the year round. This is entirely because of the clear-minded intelligence and pure thought inborn in them; since the people all have ample means of livelihood, they naturally will not stoop to base criminal conduct. Since the inborn inheritance is so fine, and the safeguarding of social morals is so strict, they are able to obtain such good results.

Looking conversely at the nations that have so much crime, the magnitude of their harm is truly beyond all words. In the single year of 1925, the lives lost to homicide in America totaled twelve thousand people; the damage suffered from crime each year amounts to about one billion dollars. Yet what is even more worrisome is that juvenile crime is increasing day by day: in 1925, of the prisoners held in the New York State courts, those between sixteen and twenty-five made up forty-six percent; in the local courts, young people of the same age bracket accounted for sixty-one percent. These youngsters all belong to a citizenry full of hope, yet they are already behind bars — truly a cause for sorrow! In 1920 I once visited the insane asylum of New York; a staff member there told me: “the mentally ill have been gradually increasing in recent years. Originally there was only this one asylum, able to hold seven thousand, but in recent years it has increased to two, able to hold fifteen thousand.” He also said: “nine-tenths of the mentally ill in the asylum are caused by venereal poison entering the brain.” With so many insane persons in a single place like New York, then the precious youth lost throughout all of America must be far more numerous still. This is a loss beyond that caused by criminals!

Besides the insane, the number of people who develop venereal disease is also not small. When I traveled in Germany, Mr. Zhang, then the acting minister, told me: “of the army students whom our government sent to study in Germany, very few have been able to serve the country upon their return; most have died of venereal poison.” I said: “I have heard that the ‘606’ injection used in Germany can cure syphilis. How could it fail to cure?” Mr. Zhang said: “salvarsan (606) indeed can cure syphilis, but its medicinal power is extremely violent; though the syphilis is cured, the heart suffers damage, so most die of heart disease.” I have several relatives: one caught venereal poison in France and died; another went insane from syphilis in America, entered a mental hospital, and was never healed for life. The number of people I myself have met who contracted venereal disease is already several; so one may imagine how great the total of such persons is. This is yet another grave loss!

Yet the present losses are still limited. As for the next generation of citizens produced by this kind of degenerating stock, the weakness of their morality and reason, the lowness of their work efficiency, and the poverty of their compassion are truly unavoidable. This loss to the nation is especially immeasurable. This is fact, not imagination. France is a nation renowned for sexual indulgence. When I traveled in Paris, I saw at the entrances and exits of the parks here and there people holding obscene pictures for sale, and the police did not intervene. Such a situation I have not seen in other countries. For thirty years the birth rate of France's population has been falling day by day — it is truly because of sexual indulgence that it has had such an enormous influence! Discussing the present state of America, the licentiousness between men and women there has probably already surpassed France, and its future gives ample cause for worry. One must not neglect the deep-set root of its disease because of temporary material prosperity. The reason I write this is not that I have leisure to worry about America, but truly that I worry about the youth of our own country who worship America! Today's Shanghai has truly already become a miniature of Paris and New York. Obscene publications, houses that entice to lust, places of dancing, morals offenses, the sharp increase of criminal cases, the overcrowding of prisons — there is not one of these that is not about to take first place in the world. For every factor of decline in France and America we now possess them all in full — then how can its miserable outcome be escaped?

Shanghai today has more than a hundred dance halls; assuming an average of two hundred people in each, then every night there are twenty thousand people — and these people are about to become the stand-ins for the various American facts described above. As the saying goes, the parties concerned are blinded. Those who are lost within it think only of the pleasure before their eyes; how would they know that this single thought of indulging in pleasure has already entered into karmic connection with prisons, insane asylums, venereal-disease hospitals, and funeral parlors. And the several relatives and friends I recounted who went mad or died from venereal disease in America and France all went for the sake of study; such a miserable ending — how could it have been foreseen at the time! One of them, before he departed for Paris, I had earnestly admonished him in advance and even alarmed him with strong words; he knew it deeply, yet in the end he could not escape dying of venereal poison. At that time he was already thirty, no longer young; and his attainments in both Chinese and Western learning were excellent, so one cannot say he was ignorant. Yet the enticement of the environment is truly not easy to withstand! So our Chinese morality lays special weight upon ritual defense, upon men and women having their separate spheres, precisely in order to prevent and avoid stirring one another's hearts! This is the lesson drawn from the experience of the facts!

Confucius said: “hearing lawsuits, I am no different from others; but what I seek is that there be no lawsuits at all.” Viewed in the light of the facts of the Netherlands, causing there to be no lawsuits is indeed possible. Confucius also said: “guide them with government and align them with penalties, and the people evadeth punishment without shame; guide them with virtue and align them with propriety, and they will have shame and will come to order.” European and American politics know only of government and penalty, and do not know of virtue and propriety, so the result is such chaos. Whereas the Netherlands is able to value propriety and teaching, so its social order produces such good results. Then those who bear the responsibility of guiding public opinion may take warning! Perhaps someone will say: “if propriety is heavy, it makes people too constrained; young people ought to have recreation to keep their spirits lively, so that their studies and their affairs may be carried on with vigor.” I shall answer him: “the conclusions reached by scientific research are precisely the opposite.”

Mr. Taylor, who invented the scientific management method in America, studied the efficiency of workers in more than thirty large factories and companies and wrote a report saying: “the efficiency of each factory and company is lowest on Mondays. Examining its cause carefully, I learned that the workers all spend Sunday dancing and indulging in pleasure! Even until Tuesday morning they cannot recover their productive efficiency.” This shows how widespread the custom and habit of dancing is in America. If the workers and employees of factories are so, then schools, shops, and public servants are no exception. Taken together, this means a diminished efficiency across the whole nation, and the greatness of the loss may be imagined. From this we can know that such recreation not only cannot keep the spirits lively, but on the contrary reduces one's energy. Nevertheless, human bodily and mental efficiency does have ways of being enhanced. For the most part, on the physical side one must train; and on the psychological side one must nurture and conserve.

Lord Zeng Wenzheng once said: “the more the spirit is used, the more it flows forth; the more wisdom is tried by hardship, the brighter it becomes.” He also said: “hold reverence and the body grows strong; practice toil and the spirit is honored.” To hold reverence means to rouse one's spirit, and in nothing to dare be remiss. When Lord Zeng Wenzheng was in the army, at dawn he shared the morning meal with his staff, and only after the second night watch did he retire; no important document was not written in his own hand; though military and civil affairs were extremely voluminous, his own reading still followed a set schedule. Tao Kan of the Jin dynasty, each morning carried a hundred tiles out beyond the house and at dusk carried them back inside, saying: “I am devoting myself to the great task of recovering the Central Plain; if in ordinary times my life were too leisurely, I fear that at the critical moment I could not bear the great responsibility, so I must compel myself to endure hardship and toil!” The great Han scholar Dong Zhongshu let down his window curtains to study, and in three years his eyes never looked upon the garden. King Goujian of Yue, sleeping upon fuel and tasting gall, strove to rouse himself to strength. From ancient times, the great men whose learning and careers achieved something all came from diligent, bitter striving — how would they use recreation as a method of nurturing the spirit? For a person's willpower must be honed and tempered before it grows stronger; if one thinks recreation indispensable, then his willpower has already grown weak first. Moreover, recreation belongs to low-grade feeling, and the loosening of the mind will then be beyond all control. If workers and employees in factories already greatly reduce their work efficiency because of it, how much more those who are charged with great responsibilities! What I have said above is the physical training.

Marquis Zhuge once said: “without detachment one cannot clarify one's purpose; without tranquility one cannot reach far.” Detachment means having few desires; all desires can darken a person's resolve, and low-grade desires are the more serious. Tranquility means the settling of the mind; if the mind is bound to emotional desires, there is no possibility of tranquility. Therefore, to preserve the keen, sharp intelligence and lively spirit of young people, the most important thing is to avoid these low-grade sensory contacts. Mencius said: “to one of few desires, though there be something not preserved, it is little; to one of many desires, though there be something preserved, it is little.” This saying refers to whether the clear, bright purpose is preserved or not. In short, when a person's cravings run deep his innate capacity is shallow; when his desires for material things are few his wisdom is clear. What has been said above is the psychological nurture.

These two points are the principles of self-cultivation of all sages and philosophers, at home and abroad, in ancient and modern times; they cannot be violated, and there is no exception. The testimonies of persons and of events cited above are all well grounded, and are not hollow theories!

And the so-called scientific outlook means observing objective facts with a cool head. The so-called materialists and New Culture advocates of today, who argue for accepting European and American culture wholesale, have all failed to observe objective facts with a settled mind, and this is also because their own cravings and desires are too many, so that they have lost their cool heads! If their subjective attitude grows strong, then the scientific outlook will vanish entirely, and then they will inevitably turn around and call me a laggard behind the times — there is nothing surprising in that!

blocks.text: Notes on Collating The Method of Preserving Wealth

inline.s: I am deeply grateful to the Honghua Society of Suzhou for giving me this opportunity to collate the text. The Method of Preserving Wealth is one of the earlier books I encountered after I began studying Buddhism, and at the time it gave me some illumination. More than a decade later, upon carefully re-reading it, I was moved even more deeply, and some of my very views on life underwent a subversive change. Now, reflecting on why I did not value it so highly then: on the one hand, my experience of life was insufficient; on the other, I did not well understand the author. Not to prize the person, and so hard to prize the teaching — this is probably a common failing.

Therefore, to help readers value this book, we collected and arranged the background materials of the author, and placed before the book, as a substitute preface, the relevant articles of the modern eminent monk Master Yinguang and the noted lyric poet Mr. Liu Yazi. If, through these materials, one comes to understand that Layman Nie Yuntai was so extraordinary, then his words will be all the easier to take to heart.

The accompanying essay of this book, The Horrors of the Brothel, may well be called the best annotation to The Method of Preserving Wealth. A son who ruins the family either gambles or frequents prostitutes. All who frequent prostitutes surely come to ruin — then what is there to speak of preserving wealth? To put it more precisely, frequenting prostitutes is not merely a matter of ruining the family; it is simply walking the road that leads to having no heir and no posterity.

In order to make people more vigilant against the harm of prostitution and to understand the way to distance themselves from it, we again collected some fine articles from the web site and the forum devoted to the precepts against sexual misconduct, combined and arranged them, and offered them to the public.

In the course of collation, I made simpler renderings of some of the more difficult classical Chinese passages, and corrected individual words and phrases. But limited by time and by my own level, there may still be deficiencies; therefore I humbly hope that the wise and learned of all quarters will point them out.

Finally, I sincerely hope that all people may remain chaste and self-respecting before marriage, faithful and harmonious after marriage, treasure the precious body bestowed by their parents, restrain desire and nourish life, and attain the happy life of wealth, longevity, health, and peace.
Shangqiu City Shoukang Culture Research Society
July
